module_title: History of Classification and the Modern Periodic Law
introduction: As more elements were discovered, scientists needed a way to organize them to make their study easier. This level covers the early historical attempts that laid the foundation for the ultimate chemistry cheat sheet.

core_concepts.title: Dobereiner's Triads (1817)
core_concepts.description:
He arranged elements with similar properties into groups of three (triads). 
Rule: The atomic mass of the middle element is approximately the 'average' of the atomic masses of the other two elements. 
Example: Lithium (Li), Sodium (Na), Potassium (K). (Li is 7, K is 39, so Na = (7+39)/2 = 23).

core_concepts.title: Newlands' Law of Octaves (1866)
core_concepts.description:
He arranged elements in increasing order of their atomic masses. 
Rule: Just like musical notes, the properties of every 'eighth' element are similar to the 'first'. (This law only worked well up to Calcium).

core_concepts.title: Mendeleev's Periodic Table (1869)
core_concepts.description:
The biggest milestone in chemistry classification. 
Rule: 'The physical and chemical properties of elements are the periodic function of their ATOMIC MASSES.' 
Brilliance: Mendeleev boldly left 'empty gaps' in his table, predicting the existence and properties of elements that hadn't been discovered yet.

core_concepts.title: The Modern Periodic Table (1913)
core_concepts.description:
Discovered by: Henry Moseley. 
Rule: 'The physical and chemical properties of elements are the periodic function of their ATOMIC NUMBERS (number of protons).' Moseley proved that atomic number, not mass, is the fundamental property of an element.

important_entities.name: Mendeleev's Predicted Elements
important_entities.significance: The elements Mendeleev predicted were later discovered and named: 'Eka-Boron' became Scandium (Sc), 'Eka-Aluminum' became Gallium (Ga), and 'Eka-Silicon' became Germanium (Ge). This is a highly repeated exam question.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Exam Trap: Examiners frequently ask what the Modern Periodic Table is based on. Remember, the old table (Mendeleev's) was based on 'Atomic Mass/Weight', but the Modern table (Moseley's) is based on 'Atomic Number'.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: B-Sc (Boron -> Scandium), Al-Ga (Aluminum -> Gallium), Si-Ge (Silicon -> Germanium).

exam_strategy_tips: A direct SSC question: 'Who gave the Modern Periodic Law?' Answer: Henry Moseley.
